title: Phenol and hydroxide
subtitle: Phenol is acidic enough for hydroxide: phenoxide forms

reactants.caption: phenol + sodium hydroxide
reactants.learnerPrompt: Draw the proton transfer from phenol to hydroxide.
hintTiers: Phenol has one acidic hydrogen. Which one, and which species is the base?
Hydroxide's lone pair makes a new O–H bond; phenol's O–H bond breaks onto its oxygen. Two arrows.
Arrow 1: a lone pair of hydroxide to the hydrogen on phenol's oxygen. Arrow 2: that O–H bond onto phenol's oxygen, which becomes negative.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The ring is electron-rich, so hydroxide does not attack it. The electron-poor atom is the hydrogen on phenol's oxygen.
Curved arrows start where the electrons are and point to where they go. Start at the base's lone pair, not at the proton.
The bond breaks towards the more electronegative atom. Hydrogen leaves as H⁺, with no electrons; the bonding pair stays on the other atom.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good start: the lone pair makes a new bond to the hydrogen. But that hydrogen now has two bonds, four electrons, and it can hold only two. Which bond must break, and where do its electrons go?

steps.explanationAfterStep: A lone pair on phenoxide's oxygen can push into the ring (an O lone pair into the C–O bond, a ring π bond onto the next carbon), so the negative charge is shared by oxygen and the ortho and para carbons. That stabilises phenoxide, so phenol is about a million times more acidic than ethanol. Hydroxide deprotonates it completely.

mechanismSummary: Hydroxide takes the O–H proton of phenol. Phenol (pKa 10) is a much stronger acid than water (pKa 15.7) because the negative charge of phenoxide spreads from oxygen into the ring, onto the ortho and para carbons.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 8 (Acidity, basicity and pKa)
